newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seeks deadly fever link with ostriches.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks deadly fever link with ostriches.

text.p: South African scientists made urgent efforts on Tuesday to find the link between ostriches and a deadly tick-borne disease that has killed one abattoir worker and put another 16 in hospital.
The outbreak of Congo-Crimean haemorrhagic fever in Oudtshoorn, capital of the lucrative South African ostrich industry, has forced a halt to slaughtering of the birds and to export of their meat.

"The export of all fresh meat has been stopped immediately while all fresh meat supplies have been removed from butcheries where possible," the Little Karoo Cooperative, which dominates the world market in ostrich products, said in a statement.
Congo fever, like the more notorious Ebola disease, causes body organs to degenerate with massive internal as well as some external bleeding. About 30 percent of Congo fever cases are fatal.
Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom said in a statement that slaughtering had been halted to protect the 350 abattoir workers in Oudtshoorn.

"Researchers believe the most probable source of infection is contact with infected ticks during the defeathering process," he said, but added it was possible that contact with fresh blood and excreta from ostriches could also cause infection.
Hanekom said tests on infected cattle showed humans would not get the disease if they ate beef that had been matured 24 hours.
"There is reason to believe (this) will be applicable to ostrich meat, which will mean that matured ostrich meat would be equally fit for human consumption. Further tests are being conducted."
A spokesman for the cooperative, Ben de Kock, said there were no recorded cases of anyone being infected with Congo fever by eating ostrich meat.
"All the researchers are trying now to establish the source of infection," he said.
De Kock said the "perfect opportunity" for an abattoir worker to contract the disease from a tick was at the start of the slaughter line where feathers are plucked by hand.

One of South Africa's top virus specialists, Bob Swanepoel, said infection could spread during the processing of hides and feathers, when ticks would jump from the ostrich skins onto the human workers.

He said blood tests had so far confirmed Congo fever in four out of 16 patients transferred from Oudtshoorn to a Cape Town hospital since the weekend. One abattoir worker died before she could be transferred.
"We don't know how the disease behaves in ostriches," Swanepoel said. "We're doing tests on ostrich chicks now."

De Kock said another 10 abattoir workers had been admitted to an Oudtshoorn hospital for observation on Tuesday after showing slight signs of fever. Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma visited the patients on Tuesday.
South Africa's first confirmed case was in 1981 in a boy bitten by a tick and since then there have been sporadic cases, mainly in rural areas.
